opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that pre-training on its own is essentially learning to imitate. You compress a huge amount of human-written text, and the model gets very good at predicting what comes next. But a lot of reasoning isn't written down. When a mathematician solves a hard problem, what ends up on paper is the clean final proof, not the dozens of dead ends, the backtracking, the "wait, that doesn't work, let me try another approach." So if you only imitate the data, you're imitating outcomes without the process that produced them.

Reinforcement learning changes the objective. Instead of asking "what would a human have written here?", you ask "did this actually get the right answer?" Once you optimize for that, the model has room to explore. It can try long chains of thought, make mistakes, notice them, and correct itself, and it gets rewarded when that process leads somewhere correct. What's interesting is that behaviors like reflection and self-verification start to emerge on their own. You don't have to hand-design them. The model discovers that checking its work is useful because it raises the reward.

The second thing I'd emphasize is that RL is a way to keep scaling when high-quality data becomes the bottleneck. The internet is finite. But if you have a good environment and a reliable reward signal, the model can generate its own training experience. In a sense you're converting compute into data. That's why I think of RL not as a fine-tuning trick at the end, but as one of the main ways to keep pushing the frontier.

That said, there are real challenges. The biggest is the reward. In math or code you can verify answers fairly cleanly, so RL works very well there. In open-ended domains like writing, research, or long agentic tasks, defining what "good" means is much harder, and if your reward is imperfect, the model will find ways to exploit it. So a lot of the important work now is building better environments and better verifiers, and figuring out how to extend these gains from domains with clear answers to messier real-world tasks.

There's also an efficiency question. Long reasoning is powerful, but you don't want the model thinking for ten thousand tokens on something simple. Teaching it to allocate thinking appropriately, going long when it's hard and short when it's easy, is part of making this practical.

So my view is that pre-training gives you the knowledge and the prior, and RL is what turns that into the ability to actually think through problems. The combination is what moves us toward models that can solve things nobody has written the answer to yet.

r001.rationale: The response presents reinforcement learning as important for scaling reasoning and says it turns pretrained knowledge into the ability to think through problems, but it does not clearly state that current methods make it difficult to achieve high intelligence without RL.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that pre-training and reinforcement learning are solving two different problems, and the reasoning limitations people see in large models mostly come from asking pre-training to do a job it was never designed for.

Pre-training is fundamentally about imitation. You take all the text humans have written and you learn to predict it. That gives you an enormous amount of knowledge and a very good prior over what a plausible next token looks like. But human text almost never records the actual process of thinking. When someone writes a math proof or a piece of code, they write down the polished result. The wrong turns, the backtracking, the moment where they realize an approach is not going to work and switch to another one, none of that is in the data. So a model trained purely on next-token prediction learns to produce answers that look like answers, but it has very little supervision on the process that generates correct answers. That is why you see models that are extremely fluent and knowledgeable but fragile on multi-step problems. They have learned the surface of reasoning, not the dynamics of it.

Reinforcement learning changes the objective. Instead of asking "does this look like what a human would write," you ask "did this actually lead to the right outcome." And once the signal is about outcomes rather than imitation, the model is free to discover its own process. You see this very concretely when you train with RL on verifiable tasks like math and code. The model starts to generate longer chains of thought on its own. It learns to check its work, to try an approach and abandon it, to decompose a problem. Nobody wrote that behavior into the training data. It emerges because those behaviors increase the probability of a correct final answer, and the reward signal rewards exactly that.

There is also a scaling story here that I find important. For a long time, scaling meant more parameters and more pre-training tokens. But high-quality human data is finite, and we are getting close to the point where simply adding more of it yields diminishing returns. RL opens up a different axis. The model generates its own trajectories, you evaluate them, and the good ones become training signal. In principle the supply of that kind of data is unbounded, as long as you have a reliable way to judge outcomes. And it also moves compute from training time into inference time. The model can spend more tokens thinking on a hard problem, and RL is what teaches it to use those tokens productively rather than just rambling.

Now, I want to be honest about the limitations. RL works beautifully when you have a clean reward, which is why math and competitive programming were the first domains to break open. The hard part is everything else. Writing, research, open-ended analysis, long-horizon agentic tasks where the outcome only becomes clear after many steps. There the reward is noisy or delayed or partly subjective, and the model becomes very good at finding whatever shortcut maximizes the reward you actually specified rather than the one you intended. A lot of the real work right now is in building reward models and verification methods that generalize beyond the domains where you can just check the answer. I think of this as the central research problem for the next few years, more than any particular architecture question.

So to answer directly: I do not think RL is a patch on top of a large model. I think it is the second half of the recipe. Pre-training compresses human knowledge into the model, and RL teaches the model how to actually use that knowledge to reach goals. If you want models that reason rather than recite, you need both, and I would say most of the frontier progress we are going to see is going to come from how far we can push the second half.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training alone leaves models fragile on multi-step problems and concludes that models need both pre-training and RL to reason rather than recite, clearly conveying that current reasoning capability requires RL alongside pre-training.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning can help by changing what we optimize for. In pretraining, a language model primarily learns to predict the next token. That gives it a lot of knowledge and some reasoning ability, but it doesn’t directly train the model to find a correct solution through a sequence of decisions.

With reinforcement learning, we can let the model try different approaches and reward successful outcomes. For example, if a math answer can be checked or a piece of code can be tested, that feedback can help the model learn when to break a problem down, check an intermediate result, or abandon an approach that isn’t working. So the opportunity is to learn how to use computation more effectively during reasoning.

The challenge is the reward. In math and coding, correctness is often relatively easy to verify. For open-ended questions, it’s much harder to distinguish a genuinely good solution from something that just sounds convincing. And even with a reliable reward, you need enough exploration to discover better strategies.

So I see reinforcement learning as a promising way to develop reasoning beyond what imitation alone can provide. But its effectiveness depends on the quality of the feedback and the problems we give the model to learn from.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls reinforcement learning promising and discusses its benefits and challenges, but does not state that current methods make it difficult for a language model to become highly intelligent without reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning can help because reasoning is not just about knowing facts. It’s also about deciding what to do next: which approach to try, when to check an assumption, and when to abandon a path that isn’t working.

Pretraining gives a language model a foundation, but its objective is to predict the next token. Reinforcement learning can push it toward a different objective: finding a correct solution. In domains like mathematics or coding, where we can verify an answer or run tests, the model can explore different approaches and learn from which ones succeed.

The challenge is the quality of that feedback. A correct final answer doesn’t necessarily mean the reasoning was sound, and a model may learn to exploit weaknesses in the reward. So we need reliable evaluation, sufficiently difficult tasks, and ways to encourage exploration without rewarding unnecessary verbosity.

I see reinforcement learning as a way to make better use of the model’s existing knowledge and potentially discover new problem-solving strategies. But the real test is whether those strategies generalize to unfamiliar problems, beyond the tasks we can easily score.

r001.rationale: The response presents reinforcement learning as helpful for improving reasoning, but does not state that current methods make it difficult for a language model to become highly intelligent without it.
